procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment of Allahabad High Court dated January 8 1963 in Civil Misc. Writ Petition No. 3160 of 1962
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Civil Misc. Writ Petition No. 3160 of 1962 was heard and a judgment was delivered on January 8, 1963.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via a Writ Petition (No. 435 of 1968) under Article 32 of the Constitution of India for the enforcement of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court disapproved of the Allahabad High Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the proviso to s. 142-A(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, gave the federal legislature the power to alter the quantum of assessment only once, or from time to time.

law: The key legal text under interpretation is the proviso to s. 142-A(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the legislature's power to alter the tax assessment could only be exercised once.
The Court's reasoning was based on a textual analysis of the proviso, specifically the phrase "unless for the time being".
According to the Court, this phrase indicates that the legislature could, at any point in time, substitute a new tax rate for the one that was currently prevailing.
This ability to act "at any point of time" implies a continuous power, not a one-time authority that is exhausted after its first use.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court concluded that the proviso gave the federal legislature the power to fix a new rate of tax in substitution for the prevailing one not just once, but from time to time.

issue.issue_text: Whether the assessment was illegal because the time schedule mentioned in rules 4 and 5 of the relevant notification was not adhered to.

facts: The assessee argued that the tax assessment was illegal because the assessing authority did not follow the time schedule prescribed in rules 4 and 5 of the relevant notification.
law: Procedural rules that set a time schedule for official work are considered 'directory' rather than 'mandatory' if there is no indication that non-compliance would cause prejudice to the affected party.
application: The Supreme Court examined rules 4 and 5, which laid down dates for the assessment work to be started and completed.
The Court determined that these rules were merely directory.
It found nothing in the rules to suggest that an assessee would be prejudiced if the dates were not strictly observed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the failure to adhere to the time schedule did not make the assessment illegal because the rules setting the schedule were directory, not mandatory.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appointment of the Kar Adhikari, who made the assessment, was valid in law.

facts: The Kar Adhikari was appointed on August 8, 1965.
The assessment in question was made on March 6, 1968, which was more than two years after the appointment.
Instead of consulting with the Public Service Commission before the appointment, the Parishad merely notified the Commission by sending them the papers after the appointment had been made.
law: Under Section 43 of the relevant Act, the appointment of an officer like the Kar Adhikari must be made by the Parishad "in consultation with the Public Service Commission."
The court defines "consultation" as a process where parties make their views known to each other and discuss them, not simply a one-way notification.
A temporary appointment is only considered effective for a maximum of two years.
application: The Court determined that merely sending papers to the Public Service Commission after the appointment did not satisfy the legal requirement of "consultation" as mandated by Section 43.
The Court also considered an alternative argument: even if the appointment were viewed as temporary, its legal validity would have expired.
Since the assessment was made more than two years after the appointment date, the officer's authority, even if temporary, had lapsed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Kar Adhikari's appointment was not valid in law. This was because the mandatory consultation with the Public Service Commission did not occur, and even if the appointment was considered temporary, its two-year effective period had expired before the assessment was made. Therefore, the assessment was made by a person not competent to do so, and the assessment order was quashed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the proviso to s. 142-A(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, gave the federal legislature the power to alter the quantum of assessment only once, or from time to time.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner relied on a passage in Craies on Statute Law to support their argument on this issue.
respondent_arguments: The text does not contain the respondent's arguments on this issue.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the assessment was illegal because the time schedule mentioned in rules 4 and 5 of the relevant notification was not adhered to.
appellant_arguments: The assessment was illegal because the time schedule specified in rules 4 and 5 of the notification of January 28 was not followed.
respondent_arguments: The rules regarding the time schedule were merely directory, not mandatory, and no prejudice was caused to the assessee by the delay.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appointment of the Kar Adhikari, who made the assessment, was valid in law.
appellant_arguments: The appointment of the Kar Adhikari was invalid as it was not made in consultation with the Public Service Commission as required by s. 43 of the U. P. Act XXXIII of 1961.
Even if it was a temporary appointment, it was only effective for two years under s. 47, and the assessment was made after that period had expired, rendering it an act by an incompetent person.
respondent_arguments: The appointment was valid because the State Government had created a Central transferable cadre and framed the U. P. Zila Parishad Central Transferable Cadre Rules, 1966, which included the Kar Adhikari's post.

cases.case_name: M.P. V. Sundararamier & Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh
cases.principle: The legislative power conferred on Parliament under Article 286(2) carries with it the authority to enact a law either prospectively or retrospectively, unless there is a limitation found within the Constitution itself.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power conferred on a Sovereign Legislature is a legislative power that carries with it the authority to enact a law either prospectively or retrospectively, unless a limitation on that power can be found in the Constitution itself.
obiter: Procedural rules that lay down a time schedule for work to be completed are merely directory and not mandatory, where there is nothing to suggest that prejudice would be caused to an assessee if the dates were not strictly observed.

The use of the expression 'unless for the time being provision to the contrary is made' in a statute grants the legislature power to act on a matter from time to time, and such power is not exhausted by a single use.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Although the petitioner's primary arguments regarding the legislature's power to tax and procedural timelines were without merit, the assessment order must be quashed because the respondents failed to demonstrate that the assessing officer, the Kar Adhikari, was validly appointed. The respondents could not prove that the appointment was made 'in consultation with' the Public Service Commission as required by statute, rendering the assessment an act by an incompetent person.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation of 'unless for the time being': The court interpreted this phrase to determine if a legislative power was a one-time event or could be exercised continuously.

Directory vs. Mandatory Rules: The court distinguished between procedural rules that are merely directory (where non-compliance does not invalidate an action, especially without prejudice) and those that are mandatory (where strict compliance is required).

Sufficient Compliance with Statutory Requirements: The court evaluated whether merely notifying a body (the Public Service Commission) of an appointment met the statutory requirement of making the appointment 'in consultation with' that body.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the proviso to s. 142-A(2) gave the legislature power to alter the assessment quantum only once was rejected as 'patently fallacious'. The court held that the expression 'unless for the time being' clearly gave the Federal Legislature power to fix a rate of tax in substitution for the prevailing one 'not only once but from time to time'.

The contention that the assessment was illegal for not adhering to the time schedule in rules 4 and 5 was rejected because the court found these rules were 'merely directory and not mandatory' and there was 'nothing in these rules to suggest that if the dates were not strictly observed any prejudice would be caused to the assessee'.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's assessment was invalidated because they failed to prove the Kar Adhikari's appointment was lawful. The court found that merely informing the Public Service Commission of the appointment and noting they had not expressed disapproval was not 'sufficient compliance with s. 43', which required the appointment to be made 'in consultation with' the Commission.
